name: Tara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crusher shift at a large bauxite mine, and I still run the control board when someone is off. The ore comes in on trucks, goes through the jaws and moves out on belts; I listen for a change in the motors before the warning light catches up. I have a two-year technical diploma and train new operators by having them walk the belts with me. My husband Omar repairs buses, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about ten months of expenses saved. I use an AI tool now and then for a parts list, once I've checked the fault myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crusher crew a faster parts list is fine, but we still have to hear a bearing fail. A small tool should earn its place beside the spanners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead job and wage would hold. Omar's bus work and our savings give us room, but I would still watch overtime because the mortgage has years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the belt walk before every shift and check any suggested part number with the maintenance book. In the first year, I'll have new operators learn that check before they touch the ordering screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the mine, not excited by another screen. I like a tool when it saves a trip, not when it tells a trainee to stop looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did your ears catch a fault before a screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a bearing sounded dry while the temperature reading stayed normal. I stopped the belt and found the grease line blocked, which a neat form would not have heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Omar we're keeping our usual mortgage payment and the children's weekend sports. There's no reason to spend our cushion just because paperwork got quicker.

say: I would accept **faster parts lists** after operators check the fault and the part number.
I would tell trainees that **motor sounds** still matter beside a screen.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to hold, with Omar’s bus work adding household security.
I would still watch **overtime** because the mortgage has several years left.
do: **Keep walking** the belts before each shift and verify part numbers in the maintenance book.
**Teach new operators** the physical check before they use an ordering screen.
feel: **Settled** about her job, with little patience for untested shortcuts.
S0.quote: A small tool should earn its place beside the spanners.
fieldNote: Her **authority** comes from detecting mechanical faults by sound and teaching that judgment on the belt walk.
A **ten-month cushion** and her husband’s bus repair income support a calm view of modest automation.

steps.text: Keep checking crusher belts before every shift
Teach new operators to verify AI part suggestions against maintenance records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may change its ordering and planning before our crusher gets a robot. I'd let the mine try a system, but every shift lead should be able to reject a bad parts order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer clerks may handle orders, and managers might expect a quicker turnaround from maintenance. My own post should remain, but rushed repairs can make the next shift dangerous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the maintenance foreman to show me the new ordering screen after his team has tested it. In the first year I'll compare the suggested spares with three actual repair jobs before I use the screen on my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious rather than afraid for our income. I want proof from real breakdowns before the crew relies on a new display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a new parts screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the screen lists the wrong bearing, I'd use the serial plate and the old maintenance book. The belt can wait; a failed bearing can damage the whole drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose a chance to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to keep an apprenticeship place in maintenance even if software makes ordering quicker. A young worker learns a lot by taking a gearbox apart.

say: I would expect **ordering and planning** to change before hands-on crusher work.
I would insist each **shift lead** can reject a parts order that fails a physical check.
think: I expect **fewer clerical tasks** and more pressure for fast maintenance turnaround.
I think my **lead post** holds, but rushed repairs could endanger the following shift.
do: **Watch a tested screen** with the maintenance foreman before using it myself.
**Compare suggested parts** with three real repair jobs during the first year.
feel: **Cautious** about repair quality, while her own household income feels safe.
S1.quote: A young worker learns a lot by taking a gearbox apart.
fieldNote: She accepts **proven technology** only after maintenance tests and serial numbers confirm suggested parts.
Her concern for **apprenticeship places** is rooted in practical learning, not an expected loss of her own wage.

steps.text: Watch the maintenance foreman test the new ordering screen
Compare AI part suggestions with three completed repair jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team thinking AI by 2028 could reorder parts and shifts, while capable crusher robots follow around 2031. The company should offer paid apprenticeships in machine maintenance before it cuts operator rosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the first blow to us could be overtime, then fewer control-board posts once robots handle the physical checks. Ten months saved helps, and Omar can still earn, but I won't assume that makes our mortgage harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll put half my overtime pay toward the mortgage and ask the mine about its paid maintenance apprenticeship. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll take an apprenticeship place only if it pays enough to keep our monthly mortgage covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my own hours and for the trainees I teach. A repair trade I know is more useful than a promise that somebody will look after us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would an apprenticeship fit the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Omar exactly what an apprentice wage would be before changing the family budget. My husband's bus repair pay isn't a blank cheque for my training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different post at the crusher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to know whether the mine will still need people to isolate a belt and inspect a jam by hand. If such posts are offered, I would consider one at a wage we can live on.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking changes** from capable crusher robots around 2031.
I would ask for **paid maintenance apprenticeships** before operator rosters are cut.
think: I could lose **overtime** first and a control-board post once robots perform physical checks.
I think our **ten-month cushion** and Omar’s wage help, but the mortgage remains an obligation.
do: **Pay extra** on the mortgage with half of each overtime payment starting now.
**Take a maintenance apprenticeship** after thinking AI arrives only if its wage covers our monthly mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about her own hours and the trainees’ next steps, with some household room to act.
S2.quote: My husband's bus repair pay isn't a blank cheque for my training.
fieldNote: She sees **2028 paperwork changes** before possible hands-on crusher robot changes around 2031.
Her **apprenticeship choice** is conditional on pay that covers the mortgage; her husband’s wage is not treated as unlimited support.

steps.text: Pay extra on the mortgage with half of each overtime payment
Take a paid maintenance apprenticeship if its wage covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give the mine time to run proper apprenticeships. I would rather see an experienced operator learn to repair a gearbox than be handed a glossy certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 51 when robots arrive, and I could move into maintenance if there is a real opening. I won't leave a higher mine wage for an unposted job just because a manager says to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll spend one Saturday a month beside the maintenance foreman on my own time, learning the gearbox overhaul. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for the paid maintenance apprenticeship if a place is open and its wage meets our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to prepare than in the fast picture. Still, I know how quickly an employer can call a training promise off when production is down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the training real to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman can show me a bearing fit and tell me when my hands are wrong. An online badge cannot teach a worker to fit a crusher gearbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about retraining with your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children they can choose a trade or college, but they should finish what they start. Watching me learn again might do more than a speech about work.

say: I would use the **five-year window** for real maintenance apprenticeships before robots might work the crusher around 2034.
I would ask the mine to teach **gearbox repair** beside skilled mechanics.
think: I think at about **51**, I could move into maintenance if a paid opening actually exists.
I would keep my **higher wage** until an apprenticeship offer covers our mortgage.
do: **Practice gearbox work** with the maintenance foreman one Saturday each month this year.
**Apply** for a paid apprenticeship after thinking AI arrives if a place opens and the wage covers our mortgage.
feel: **More prepared**, while doubtful that an employer will always keep its training promises.
S3.quote: An online badge cannot teach a worker to fit a crusher gearbox.
fieldNote: She calculates **2034 robot arrival** at about age 51 and prefers a related trade to vague flexibility.
Her **application** depends on an open paid place and a mortgage-covering wage; Saturday practice alone is not a career move.

steps.text: Practice gearbox repair monthly with the maintenance foreman
Apply for an open paid apprenticeship if its wage covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team 2036 changes the paperwork, while capable crusher robots come around 2039. A decade gives us time to pay off debts and teach the next crew a trade that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots arrive, and we could have most of the mortgage gone if our wages hold. I might choose fewer shifts then, but I wouldn't promise retirement until the figures are in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the crusher shift and making our scheduled mortgage payments, then set an annual evening with Omar to review the pension estimate. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll compare any offered maintenance role with the pension estimate before deciding whether to cut shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our house with ten years to plan. I would still miss the noise and the crew if the crusher stopped needing operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your husband’s pay falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Omar's workshop loses bus contracts, I will keep full shifts while they are available. I won't build a family plan on one person's good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach trainees before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trainees to learn the machine's noises while they can, even if robots arrive later. Those sounds help a mechanic know where to start.

say: I would use the **decade** before capable crusher robots around 2039 to teach repairs and reduce debt.
I would urge trainees to learn **machine sounds** before relying on automatic fault reports.
think: I think at **56**, I might cut shifts if both incomes hold and the mortgage is nearly gone.
I will wait for **pension figures** before promising any retirement date.
do: **Keep leading** crusher shifts, make scheduled mortgage payments and review the pension estimate yearly with Omar.
**Compare any offered role** with the pension estimate after thinking AI arrives before reducing shifts.
feel: **Calm** about the house, with sadness at the possible loss of the crusher crew.
S4.quote: I won't build a family plan on one person's good year.
fieldNote: She treats **2039 robot arrival** at age 56 as a possible point for fewer shifts, conditional on both incomes.
Her **retirement choice** stays open until she reviews pension figures and any actual maintenance offer.

steps.text: Keep leading crusher shifts and making scheduled mortgage payments
Compare any offered maintenance role with pension figures after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the crusher could lose overtime before capable robots arrive around 2031. A paid maintenance apprenticeship with a mortgage-covering wage would help; I do not want a promise that sends the bill to my husband.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a trainee learns a sound they have never heard. A skilled mechanic must stand beside a trainee when the gearbox comes apart. I would keep real machinery in the apprenticeship.

headlineQuote: A skilled mechanic must stand beside a trainee when the gearbox comes apart.
portrait: **Tara Okafor**, 43, leads a crusher shift at a large bauxite mine and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She has **ten months saved**, a higher mine wage and a bus-mechanic husband, with two children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** for parts suggestions after checking physical faults, and wants trainees to learn motor sounds.
She favours **paid apprenticeships** and practical work over vague promises of help if robots reduce operator posts.
Across the pictures, she protects the **mortgage** and considers fewer shifts only when household income and pension figures allow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because overtime could fall before capable crusher robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance apprenticeship** covering the mortgage would let her change roles without shifting the cost to Omar.
